ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Consultation — Josephine Baker — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review: echocardiogram, cardiology consultation the same day, the cause of the breathlessness and the antiplatelet plan

text.paragraph: Breathlessness and tiredness three weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery, in a 62-year-old woman. Please assess the cause of the breathlessness and her heart function, review her antiplatelet therapy and other medicines, and advise on cardiac rehabilitation and a return to performing on stage. [S]
Urgency: Soon; on the day of her two-week visit, after the echocardiogram that morning. [S]

list.item: What is causing her breathlessness: reduced heart function, ongoing ischemia, a medicine effect, or deconditioning?
What does the echocardiogram show, and does she need further testing now?
Is ticagrelor the right P2Y12 inhibitor for her, and for how long should she take dual antiplatelet therapy?
Do you agree with metoprolol and lisinopril, and what blood pressure and LDL targets do you advise, given her lipoprotein(a) result?
When and how can she return to singing and dancing on stage, and does she need an exercise test first?
How should her hysterectomy and possible early menopause, and her sex, change our approach to her risk?

text.paragraph: Ms. Baker, a 62-year-old singer and dancer, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nwosu five weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery. She waited until the morning to go to hospital, thinking the pressure in her chest was the strain of losing her home. Since discharge she has had episodes of air hunger, a sudden need to take a deep breath, often while sitting or talking, beginning two or three days after leaving the hospital; they do not build with effort and come with no chest pressure, palpitations, orthopnea, cough or ankle swelling. Two cardiac rehabilitation sessions have not been limited by breath. She takes all her medicines and has not needed nitroglycerin. She has never smoked. She gave a clear account and asked to understand each choice. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: She was born Freda Josephine McDonald on June 3, 1906, in St. Louis, Missouri, to Carrie McDonald and Eddie Carson, into a family with little money. [D]
She grew up in poor neighborhoods of St. Louis and began working as a child; she married twice before the age of 16 and kept the surname of her second husband, William Howard Baker. [D]

She danced in New York in the musicals Shuffle Along and The Chocolate Dandies, came to Paris with her troupe in 1925 to perform at the Théâtre des Champs-Elysées, and became the most famous and highest-paid American performer in France. [D]
She married a Frenchman in 1937 and became a French citizen; the National Park Service gives 1936. [D]

During the Second World War she worked for the intelligence services of Free France with the rank of sub-lieutenant, gathering information and carrying messages written in invisible ink on her sheet music; on August 18, 1961, she received the Legion of Honor and the Croix de guerre with palm. [D]

She bought a château at Les Milandes in the Périgord, where she made a "village of the world" and raised twelve children of different nationalities and religions whom she had adopted during her tours with Jo Bouillon, her husband; the children were called the "Rainbow Tribe". [D]

In North Africa during the war she was taken urgently to hospital in Casablanca, where she stayed in bed from June 1941 to December 1942, had five operations and was several times reported to be dying; she continued her intelligence work from her room. [D]

The illness followed the loss of a pregnancy in 1941, given as a stillbirth in Casablanca by one source and as a miscarriage by another; the second account says a severe infection required a hysterectomy, after which she developed peritonitis and septicemia. La Croix says she was unable to have children. [R]
At the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August 28, 1963, she was one of the few women to speak; she came in her military uniform with her decorations. [D]

Les Milandes ran into heavy debt; she toured repeatedly to pay it, and on June 2, 1964, she made a televised appeal for donations, saying her work no longer covered debts of about 200 million old francs. [D]

In March 1969, after a court ordered her eviction, she was removed from the château and sat for seven hours in the rain on its steps; she had a new heart attack and ended the day in hospital in Périgueux. Les Milandes was sold at auction that year. [D]

observationRange.text: 125 nmol/L or higher is a risk-enhancing level

list.item: Cause of the breathlessness (T45.525A). Ticagrelor-related breathlessness, with some deconditioning. The pattern is typical: air hunger at rest beginning within days of the start, without effort-related chest symptoms, with a normal oxygen saturation, clear lungs, normal filling pressures and no anemia. It is not a sign of heart damage or of a blocked stent, but it is distressing and leads some patients to stop their medicine. There is no sign of heart failure or of ongoing ischemia. [S]

Heart function and further testing (I25.10). The ejection fraction of 52% with inferior hypokinesis matches the infarct in the right coronary territory; function is at the lower limit of normal. No further imaging or stress testing is needed now. Repeat the echocardiogram only if her symptoms change. [S]

Antiplatelet therapy (I25.10). Ticagrelor is preferred over clopidogrel after an acute coronary syndrome, but changing to clopidogrel is appropriate when ticagrelor causes breathlessness that affects adherence. Change with a 600 mg loading dose of clopidogrel 24 hours after the last ticagrelor dose, then 75 mg daily, without a gap. Her bleeding risk is not high, so dual antiplatelet therapy should continue for twelve months from the infarction, then aspirin 81 mg alone. [S]

Beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and targets (I10). Metoprolol succinate is appropriate for the first year after the infarction and, because she has high blood pressure, beyond it. Lisinopril is indicated for high blood pressure; raise it to 10 mg for a target below 130/80 mmHg, with potassium and creatinine one to two weeks later. LDL goal below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall; her lipoprotein(a) of 172 nmol/L is an inherited risk-enhancing factor that statins do not lower, so reaching the LDL goal matters more, and ezetimibe should be added if LDL stays at 70 mg/dL or higher. [S]

Return to the stage. She can begin light dance practice within the rehabilitation program now. Before full performances, which can demand 6 to 9 METs, a symptom-limited exercise test at about twelve weeks, on her usual medicines, will set her exercise prescription and show whether she can perform safely. [S]

Women's risk factors (Z90.710). A hysterectomy in her thirties, and a possible early menopause if ovarian function was lost, add to her risk and are recorded as risk-enhancing factors. Hormone therapy is not used to prevent heart disease. Women are less often given full secondary prevention and cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack, and more often have breathlessness, tiredness or other symptoms besides chest pain; her plan should be complete, and her account of her symptoms taken seriously. Screening for depression, which is common after a heart attack and worsens outcomes, is appropriate. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nwosu's intake note and the hospital discharge summary: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, 90% mid right coronary artery stenosis with one drug-eluting stent, mild disease elsewhere, LDL 146 mg/dL. ECG at intake: sinus rhythm, small Q waves in II, III and aVF, no acute change. Echocardiogram this morning: ejection fraction 52%, hypokinesis of the basal and mid inferior wall, normal right ventricle, normal estimated filling pressures, no thrombus, normal valves. Intake laboratory tests: hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 264, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL (eGFR 81), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, LDL 84 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%. Lipoprotein(a) 172 nmol/L. Home blood pressure average 136/82. [S]

list.item: Stop ticagrelor; start clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose 24 hours after the last ticagrelor dose, then 75 mg daily. [S]

Continue aspirin 81 mg; dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months from the infarction, then aspirin 81 mg alone; never interrupt it without speaking to cardiology, and manage minor bleeding without stopping it. [S]
Continue atorvastatin 80 mg; lipid panel four to eight weeks after the start; add ezetimibe if LDL is 70 mg/dL or higher. [S]
Continue metoprolol succinate 25 mg; raise lisinopril to 10 mg daily; potassium and creatinine in one to two weeks; target below 130/80 mmHg. [S]
Complete all 36 sessions of cardiac rehabilitation, with light dance practice there. [S]
Symptom-limited exercise test at about twelve weeks before a return to full performances. [S]
No repeat echocardiogram, stress imaging or angiography unless symptoms change. [S]
Repeat the PHQ-9 at about twelve weeks; use the rehabilitation program's psychologist. [S]
Influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal and RSV vaccination as due. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ashby-Nwosu, who saw her the same day. The cause of the breathlessness, the change of antiplatelet medicine and the reasons for each other medicine were explained to Ms. Baker, who agreed to the change to clopidogrel and the higher dose of lisinopril. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Ashby-Nwosu continues her care and will send the exercise test result. Cardiology review before clopidogrel is stopped at twelve months, or sooner for chest pain, worsening breathlessness or bleeding. [S]
